title: Neuropathic Pain: From Mechanisms to Therapeutic Interventions.
abstract: Neuropathic pain is caused by injury or disease of the somatosensory system. It involves peripheral nerve injury, central sensitization, transmitter imbalance, glial activation, and large-scale network remodeling. Despite substantial advances in pain biology, clinical assessment continues to rely predominantly on patient-reported symptoms, sensory examination, and conventional neurophysiological testing, approaches that often fail to delineate the predominant biological mechanisms underlying pain in individual patients. Recent advances in sensory phenotyping and multimodal imaging have enabled in vivo characterization of abnormalities at the receptor, neuroinflammatory, and circuit levels, thereby providing a foundation for mechanism-based stratification and more individualized therapeutic decision-making. This review summarizes neuropathic pain from clinical stratification to mechanism-based imaging and therapeutic intervention. We describe key clinical dimensions, including sensory gain, sensory loss, peripheral and central pain generators, mixed nociceptive-neuropathic pain, central sensitization, and autonomic or small-fiber modifiers. These dimensions help explain why patients with the same diagnosis may show different symptoms and treatment responses. We also review major molecular mechanisms, including glutamatergic overactivity, GABAergic and glycinergic disinhibition, monoaminergic remodeling, and neuroimmune modulation. These changes reshape spinal, thalamocortical, limbic, salience, reward, cerebellar, and descending control circuits. Peripheral nerve ultrasound and MR neurography can help identify structural peripheral pain generators. PET, MRS, MRI, DTI, fMRI, EEG, and multimodal imaging can assess receptor availability, neurotransmitter balance, neuroinflammation, white matter integrity, and network connectivity. These imaging tools may link clinical phenotypes with biological mechanisms and help define mechanism-based subtypes. Imaging biomarkers may also support treatment selection, treatment monitoring, neuromodulation targeting, and translational trial design. This framework supports a shift from symptom-based assessment to mechanism-guided precision care for neuropathic pain.

title: Integrated Multi-Time-Point <sup>18</sup>F-FAPI PET/CT and Immune Histopathology for Predicting Pathological Complete Response in Microsatellite-Stable Locally Advanced Rectal Cancer Treated With Neoadjuvant Radiotherapy, Chemotherapy, and Immunotherapy.
abstract: Predicting pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant short-course radiotherapy combined with immunotherapy and chemotherapy remains challenging in microsatellite-stable (MSS) locally advanced rectal cancer. In this prospective exploratory study (ClinicalTrials.gov identifier: NCT06608537), 49 patients received short-course radiotherapy followed by sintilimab plus CAPOX and subsequently underwent radical surgery. We investigated whether treatment response could be better characterized by integrating two complementary biological dimensions: baseline immune organization and treatment-related stromal remodeling captured by multi-time-point 1 8 F-FAPI PET/CT. The pCR rate was 49.0% (24/49), and serial 1 8 F-FAPI imaging revealed distinct stromal kinetic patterns between response groups. Integration of intratumoral tertiary lymphoid structure (iTLS) count, B-cell density, preoperative tumor-to-iliacus muscle ratio (TIMR) at 30 min, and the delayed TIMR retention index from 90 to 120 min (RI 34 ) yielded a four-variable model with a mean AUC of 0.874 in repeated nested cross-validation. Complementary preclinical experiments provided functional support for a CAF-TGFβ-B-cell/TLS axis linking stromal regulation, immune organization, and treatment resistance. These findings highlight the complementary value of spatial immune organization and dynamic FAPI-defined stromal kinetics and provide a biologically informed framework for post-neoadjuvant, preoperative response stratification, pending prospective multicenter validation.

title: The Bird's Nest Sign as an Initial Presentation of Primary Pulmonary B-Cell Non-Hodgkin Lymphoma With Plasmacytic Differentiation.
abstract: The bird's nest sign (BNS) has been described as a sign on chest computed tomography (CT) in various pulmonary diseases. We report a rare case of primary pulmonary B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation presenting with BNS, mimicking an invasive fungal disease at first. A 61-year-old Vietnamese man with a history of idiopathic thrombocytopenia and splenectomy 3 years prior to admission presented with prolonged dry cough, mild dyspnoea on exertion and chest discomfort for 3 weeks. His laboratory tests were unremarkable, but his chest CT showed bilateral consolidation with the BNS. After an unfavourable response to anti-fungal therapy, the second transthoracic lung biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of primary pulmonary B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation. This case highlights the importance of considering lymphoma in the differential diagnosis of BNS when infection is excluded and concurrently seeking a confirmatory diagnosis with repeated diagnostic procedures when necessary.

title: Recent Advances in Wearable Ultrasound Patches for Healthcare Applications.
abstract: Wearable ultrasound patches, as a transformative innovation redefining the boundaries of traditional ultrasound medicine, signify a shift from hospital-centered, episodic diagnosis and therapy toward portable, personalized, and continuous healthcare solutions. As an emerging and rapidly evolving research direction, fully integrated wearable ultrasound platforms-synergistically combining real-time imaging, closed-loop sensing, and on-demand therapeutic intervention within a single conformal patch and system-have been progressively utilized for chronic disease management and closed-loop neuromodulation. This review summarizes and discusses the advanced wearable ultrasound technologies to provide insight into the underlying strategies that enable the convergence of diagnosis and therapy in diverse disease scenarios. This review primarily focuses on wearable ultrasound patches and systems for cardiovascular monitoring, musculoskeletal assessment, neurological treatment, sonodynamic therapy, drug delivery, and integrated theranostics. In addition, the challenges and development prospects of wearable ultrasound patches are analyzed to promote further clinical translation, with emphasis on the synergistic optimization of imaging and therapy, long-term integration reliability, and fully integrated portable designs. It is earnestly expected that this kind of flexible-electronics-enabled wearable ultrasound technology will stimulate comprehensive investigation and promote the clinical development of next-generation multifunctional theranostic platforms.

title: A case report of pediatric Gardner syndrome and literature review.
abstract: This case report discusses the diagnosis and treatment of a 14-year-8-month-old male patient genetically diagnosed with Gardner syndrome (GS), systematically reviewing the disease's epidemiology, clinical manifestations, imaging advances, and management strategies. The patient presented with a post-influenza A chest wall mass and had prior resections of abdominal/scalp masses. Colonoscopy revealed > 20 adenomatous polyps. Imaging demonstrated multiple craniofacial osteomas and epidermoid cysts. Genetic testing identified a pathogenic APC gene mutation (NM_000038.6:c.4669_4670del (p.Ile1557*) heterozygous variant). GS, a familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) subtype, has an estimated pediatric incidence of 1/8000-1/14,000. Its classic triad comprises colorectal polyps, osteomas, and soft tissue tumors. Recent studies indicate earlier malignant transformation of duodenal polyps in children versus adults, with desmoid tumor incidence reaching 10-20%. In imaging, low-dose CT, panoramic radiography, and contrast-enhanced MRI can improve early detection of bone lesions and soft tissue tumors. Genetic testing (APC/MUTYH) is the pediatric screening gold standard. Optimized chemoprevention (sulindac/celecoxib) and endoscopic monitoring have significantly improved prognoses. This case highlights the urgency of multidisciplinary management and genetic counseling for pediatric GS.

title: Machine learning-assisted monitoring of radiofrequency ablation in hepatic tumors using spectral traces.
abstract: Purpose Accurate intraoperative assessment of radiofrequency ablation (RFA) margins in hepatic malignancies remains a significant clinical challenge. Methods This study investigates the efficacy of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for objective, spatially resolved discrimination of ablated tissue, viable tumor, and normal parenchyma in 10 ex vivo liver specimens. Analysis of visible-near-infrared (VNIR) reflectance revealed distinct spectral signatures, characterized by a consistent monotonic hierarchy (ablated < normal < tumor), enabling reliable tissue differentiation. Segmentation performance was systematically evaluated using four supervised classifiers: Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). The total delineated tissue area exhibited notable inter-method variability, ranging from 137,283 to 189,289 pixels (+ 37.9%), underscoring sensitivity to classifier architecture. Results Nevertheless, all approaches maintained biologically coherent tissue distributions, with normal parenchyma predominating (44-56%), followed by tumor (25-39%) and ablated regions (17-20%). Purpose

Accurate intraoperative assessment of radiofrequency ablation (RFA) margins in hepatic malignancies remains a significant clinical challenge.

Methods

This study investigates the efficacy of hyperspectral imaging (HSI) for objective, spatially resolved discrimination of ablated tissue, viable tumor, and normal parenchyma in 10 ex vivo liver specimens. Analysis of visible-near-infrared (VNIR) reflectance revealed distinct spectral signatures, characterized by a consistent monotonic hierarchy (ablated < normal < tumor), enabling reliable tissue differentiation. Segmentation performance was systematically evaluated using four supervised classifiers: Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Random Forest (RF), and Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). The total delineated tissue area exhibited notable inter-method variability, ranging from 137,283 to 189,289 pixels (+ 37.9%), underscoring sensitivity to classifier architecture.

Results

Nevertheless, all approaches maintained biologically coherent tissue distributions, with normal parenchyma predominating (44-56%), followed by tumor (25-39%) and ablated regions (17-20%). That is consistently indicating the necessity for monitoring ablative margins. SAM, SVM, and LDA classifiers achieved class-specific detection errors around 3.5% and 18%. LDA attained the highest overall accuracy (94.5%), demonstrating the potential of HSI for reliable, intraoperative image-guided tissue characterization. Dimensionality reduction across 462 spectral bands identified an optimal discriminative window within 643-698 nm, supporting the development of streamlined multispectral systems.

Conclusion

Overall, HSI is neither a contact nor destructive modality for quantitative RFA assessment. Despite classifier-dependent variability necessitating standardized or ensemble strategies, these findings support its prospective integration into real-time surgical guidance, pending in vivo validation.

title: Predicting advanced-stage recurrence in resected hepatocellular carcinoma using preoperative gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI radiomics.
abstract: Objectives To develop and validate a preoperative gadoxetic acid-enhanced MRI-based radiomics model for predicting the time to advanced-stage recurrence in patients undergoing resection for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Materials and methods This retrospective single-center study included patients with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) stage 0/A HCC who underwent resection between 2009 and 2014. Patients were temporally divided into training (n = 272; 2009-2011) and validation (n = 210; 2012-2014) cohorts. Time to advanced-stage recurrence was defined as the interval from resection to macrovascular invasion and/or extrahepatic metastasis. Two radiologists segmented tumors on hepatobiliary phase images, followed by 3-mm peritumoral expansion and propagation to co-registered dynamic T1- and T2-weighted images. After extraction of Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative-compliant features, a radiomics model was developed using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-Cox regression. Model performance and inter-reader reproducibility of binary risk stratification were evaluated using the concordance index (C-index) and Cohen's kappa, respectively. Results Five-year advanced-stage recurrence occurred in 15% of the training (42/272) and validation (32/210) cohorts. In the validation cohort, the radiomics model yielded a C-index of 0.716 (95% CI, 0.631-0.801). This outperformed the preoperative BCLC (0.597; 95% CI 0.551-0.644) and Hong Kong Liver Cancer (0.594; 95% CI 0.516-0.672) staging systems, and was equivalent to the postoperative clinicopathological model (0.716; 95% CI 0.626-0.807). Radiomic-based risk stratification showed good inter-reader reproducibility (kappa = 0.757). Conclusion The preoperative radiomics model outperformed staging systems and was comparable to the postoperative clinicopathological model in predicting advanced-stage recurrence, relying entirely on noninvasive data.

title: Limited incremental value and cross-cohort transferability of CT radiomics for survival prediction after TACE in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Purpose To evaluate whether pretreatment CT radiomics adds information for overall survival (OS) prediction among patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) treated with transarterial chemoembolization (TACE), and assess frozen imaging-model performance in an independent cohort. Methods This retrospective study included 221 WAW-TACE and 98 HCC-TACE-SEG patients with pretreatment arterial and portal venous CT. Incremental value of a tumor-radiomics Random Survival Forest score (R1) beyond cohort-specific clinical Cox models (C0) was evaluated within each cohort using 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times. External validation was restricted to frozen WAW-trained R1 models (Top-K = 5, 10, 15) applied to HCC-TACE-SEG without refitting; the combined C0 + R1 model was not externally validated. Results WAW-TACE included 162 deaths and HCC-TACE-SEG 86 deaths. In WAW-TACE, C0, R1 Top-K = 15, and C0 + R1 achieved C-indices of 0.646 ± 0.043, 0.593 ± 0.049, and 0.639 ± 0.045, respectively. Corresponding HCC-TACE-SEG estimates were 0.496 ± 0.087, 0.530 ± 0.072, and 0.495 ± 0.094. Thus, R1 did not consistently improve cohort-specific clinical reference models. In frozen external application, Top-K = 5, 10, and 15 achieved C-indices of 0.463 (95% CI 0.397-0.532), 0.535 (0.468-0.608), and 0.528 (0.460-0.598), respectively. Conclusion The evaluated models showed no consistent incremental value for OS prediction within these TACE cohorts and limited frozen-model discrimination in the clinically distinct HCC-TACE-SEG cohort. These findings do not support clinical use of these models or establish a general limitation of CT radiomics.

title: Restaging the primary tumor in localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma after systemic therapy: a scoping review of the role of CT, FDG-PET, and CA19-9.
abstract: Objectives The introduction of improved multi-agent systemic therapies has made restaging and treatment response assessment in patients with localized pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) increasingly complex. This scoping review aims to assess and compare methods for local disease restaging and treatment response assessment in localized PDAC, with a focus on their association with resectability, overall survival (OS), and R0-resection rates. Materials and methods This scoping review included studies on restaging in patients with PDAC following systemic therapy using CT and PET/CT from MEDLINE, Embase, and CENTRAL. Results Among 4680 identified studies, 20 fulfilled the eligibility criteria. Most (n = 15) studies analyzed CT, and 5 analyzed PET/CT. Groups of restaging methods included new response categories, size-based metrics, volume, vascular contact, tumor attenuation, fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose ( 18 F-FDG) PET/CT derived metabolic parameters, and resectability criteria. Dual-energy CT-derived extracellular volume (DECT-ECV) was evaluated as a baseline predictive biomarker. Associations between restaging methods and outcomes were reported inconsistently: some studies found significant associations for specific methods, whereas others did not. No restaging method showed a consistent association with both R0-resection and survival across all studies. Conclusion Restaging of localized PDAC after systemic treatment remains challenging due to the limited accuracy of RECIST 1.1, particularly for the classifications partial response and stable disease. The current evidence suggests that integrating additional imaging features, alternative imaging modalities, and the biomarker carbohydrate antigen (CA)19-9 may improve the assessment of resectability and prognosis. These findings support a future version of RECIST 1.1 to alert clinicians to this issue. Key points Question How effective are current (PET/)CT-based restaging methods in assessing local disease resectability and prognosis in localized PDAC after modern multi-agent systemic therapy? Findings Current restaging methods show inconsistent association with R0-resection and survival; RECIST 1.1 is particularly limited for the assessment of partial response and stable disease. Clinical relevance Current evidence confirms a need to integrate additional imaging features and the biomarker CA19-9, during restaging in patients with localized pancreatic cancer after modern systemic therapy to improve accuracy and reduce the risk of missed treatment options.

title: Atypical presacral masses in Currarino syndrome: a case series.
abstract: Introduction Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. While anterior meningoceles and teratomas are the most commonly reported lesions, an expanding body of literature suggests a broader spectrum of presacral pathology. We present three cases from our institution that expand the phenotypic range of presacral masses associated with Currarino syndrome, including lesions not previously well described in this population. Case presentation Three cases are presented. Final pathologic diagnoses included myxopapillary ependymoma, mature cystic teratoma, and neuroendocrine tumor arising within a teratoma. Conclusion These cases highlight the considerable heterogeneity of presacral lesions in Currarino syndrome and identify two underrecognized or previously unreported tumor types: myxopapillary ependymoma and neuroendocrine tumor. Surgical management must be individualized and often requires a multidisciplinary approach. Future studies will further clarify genotype-phenotype relationships and improve diagnostic and management strategies in this complex syndrome. Established facts Currarino syndrome is a rare congenital disorder classically defined by the triad of sacral anomaly, anorectal malformation, and a presacral mass. Presacral masses are most commonly anterior meningoceles and teratomas. A wider spectrum of lesions has been reported, underscoring the complexity of the syndrome and the importance of thorough evaluation and management of presacral pathology. Novel insights In Case 1, we report a previously undescribed association of myxopapillary ependymoma with a retrorectal teratoma in the setting of Currarino syndrome. Case 2 illustrates the potential for significant enlargement of presacral meningoceles with associated teratomas with a rare instance of prenatal diagnosis by ultrasound. Case 3 expands the spectrum of presacral pathology in Currarino syndrome by demonstrating a neuroendocrine tumor.

title: Notch-referenced mediolateral verification of tibial tunnel position in anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: a 3D imaging validation study.
abstract: Background Non-anatomic tibial tunnel placement remains a leading contributor to anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR) failure. Mediolateral (ML) tunnel positioning is particularly difficult intraoperatively because no consistent bony landmark defines the lateral footprint border. Purpose To evaluate the accuracy of a novel intraoperative Notch-Referenced Mediolateral (NRML) verification technique by comparing the ML position of the tibial tunnel center (TTC) on postoperative 3D CT with the native tibial footprint center (TFC) on preoperative 3D MRI. Methods In this retrospective cross-sectional study, 108 consecutive patients underwent primary all-inside single-bundle ACLR with intraoperative NRML verification. This arthroscopic technique uses the intercondylar notch as a visual reference to verify mediolateral tibial tunnel position before definitive drilling. TFC and TTC were independently measured on preoperative 3D MRI and postoperative 3D CT using a standardized quadrant-grid protocol by two blinded observers. The primary outcome was ML deviation (tunnel - footprint). MRI-CT agreement and measurement reliability were assessed with intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Bland-Altman analysis. Results The anatomical TFC was located at 46.1 ± 2.3% of tibial plateau width in the ML direction, versus 44.8 ± 2.0% for the TTC. Mean ML deviation was -1.01 ± 1.52 mm (p < 0.001), a small but statistically significant medial bias; 91.7% (95% CI 84.9-95.6%) of tunnels fell within ±3 mm of the native footprint. MRI-CT agreement was good (ICC 0.81-0.85), and inter/intraobserver reliability was good to excellent (ICC 0.78-0.89). No significant associations were found between ML deviation and sex, injury chronicity, graft diameter, or plateau size. Conclusion In this single-arm cohort,NRML verification is a simple, equipment-free technique that placed the tibial tunnel within ~1 mm of the native ML footprint, with high measurement reliability. Prospective comparative and outcome studies are needed to confirm its clinical value. Level of evidence IV.

In this single-arm cohort,NRML verification is a simple, equipment-free technique that placed the tibial tunnel within ~1 mm of the native ML footprint, with high measurement reliability. Prospective comparative and outcome studies are needed to confirm its clinical value.

Level of evidence

IV.

title: Improved assessment of the cochlear implant and temporal bone structures with ultra-high resolution photon-counting detector CT compared to conventional CT systems.
abstract: Purpose This study evaluates the image quality of photon-counting detector CT (PCD-CT) compared to conventional CT systems in cochlear implant imaging and aims to determine optimal scan parameters. Methods Three cochlear implant models were inserted into three post-mortem human specimen heads. Each head was scanned on three high-end CT systems: SOMATOM Edge, SOMATOM Force and NAEOTOM Alpha. A total of 192 reconstructions were obtained, including various tube voltages (120-150 kV), tin filtering, and slice thicknesses (0.2-0.6 mm). For each scanner, multiple reconstruction kernels were applied. Contrast-to-noise ratios (CNR) for bone-to-soft-tissue were calculated. Two radiologists independently assessed anatomy, implant visibility, and overall image quality on a 5-point Likert scale and scored diagnostic confidence for detecting anatomic dehiscence. Results PCD-CT showed significantly higher image quality scores across implant, anatomy, and general image quality compared to the Edge and Force (p < 0.001). PCD-CT also produced significantly higher CNR (mean 23.5 vs. 13.8 [Edge] and 12.7 [Force]) and greater diagnostic confidence. For PCD-CT, optimal image quality was achieved using 0.2 mm slice thickness and the Hr89 kernel at 140 kV. PCD-CT scans acquired with half dose (27.5 mGy) showed no significant difference in CNRs but led to slightly lower subjective scores compared to standard-dose imaging. Conclusion PCD-CT provides superior image quality and diagnostic confidence in cochlear implant imaging compared to the Edge and Force. Optimal results are achieved using 140 kV, 0.2 mm slices, and the Hr89 kernel. Although dose reduction is feasible, it slightly compromises subjective image quality.

title: Artificial intelligence-based prediction of cerebrospinal fluid leak in skull base surgery: a scoping review.
abstract: Background Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leak remains one of the most significant complications of skull base surgery, particularly in endoscopic endonasal and transsphenoidal approaches. Accurate risk stratification may improve surgical planning and reconstruction strategies. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based models have been increasingly investigated for CSF leak prediction; however, the evidence remains methodologically heterogeneous. This scoping review aimed to map the current literature and summarize data sources, modeling approaches, validation strategies, and reported performance. Methods This scoping review followed PRISMA-ScR guidance. Eligibility was structured using the Population-Concept-Context framework. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for English-language studies published from 2019 to 2025. Two authors independently screened titles/abstracts and full texts and independently charted data using a standardized table; disagreements were resolved by consensus. Eligible original human studies applied AI/ML to predict perioperative surgical CSF leak or to derive an imaging biomarker for identifying spontaneous lateral skull-base CSF leak/encephalocele relevant to surgical assessment. No formal protocol was prepared or registered. Results Fifty-five records were identified, and nine primary studies met the eligibility criteria after duplicate removal and full-text assessment. Six studies predicted intraoperative CSF leak, two predicted postoperative leak, and one evaluated a deep-learning-derived CT biomarker for identifying spontaneous lateral skull-base CSF leak or encephalocele relevant to surgical assessment. Three studies used classical machine-learning methods, four used predominantly deep neural-network or convolutional-neural-network approaches, one compared classical models with a feedforward neural network, and one used a BERT-based natural-language-processing model. One study reported prospective temporal validation; none reported independent external validation at another institution. Among studies reporting AUC, values ranged from 0.69 to 1.00; accuracy, where reported, ranged from 70% to 98.33%. Conclusions AI-based prediction of CSF leak is a promising but evolving field. Methodological heterogeneity and the absence of independent external validation constrain clinical translation. Future studies should prioritize standardized outcomes, multicenter datasets, and prospective validation to support integration into clinical decision-making.

title: Selective preoperative lower extremity computed tomography angiography before mandibular reconstruction: Identifying patients unlikely to require fibula free flap reconstruction.
abstract: Purpose Not every patient undergoing mandibular continuity resection requires free fibula flap (FFF) reconstruction. Whether clinical judgment reliably identifies patients unlikely to benefit from preoperative lower-extremity computed tomography angiography (CTA) remains unknown, despite the relevance of this question for cost-conscious and resource-efficient imaging strategies. Methods A retrospective outcome-based validation was conducted in patients undergoing mandibular continuity resection between July 2012 and June 2023. The primary outcome was secondary FFF reconstruction among patients not initially selected for CTA. Factors associated with CTA utilization were assessed by multivariable logistic regression. Results 316 consecutively operated patients were included. Prior radiotherapy (OR 2.67, p = 0.005) and smoking history (OR 1.98, p = 0.032) were independently associated with CTA utilization. Among 111 patients without primary FFF reconstruction, four (3.6%) required secondary FFF reconstruction, all of whom had undergone CTA. No patient managed without CTA subsequently required FFF reconstruction. Conclusions In this cohort, clinical judgment was associated with successful identification of patients who did not subsequently require fibular reconstruction. Omission of CTA in carefully selected patients was not associated with subsequent reconstructive deficiency, though larger prospective studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: First report of proven Fusarium brachygibbosum sinusitis in a paediatric patient with acute myeloblastic leukaemia.
abstract: Purpose Fusarium brachygibbosum is an environmental mould belonging to the Fusarium sambucinum species complex (FSAMSC) and is only exceptionally reported as a human pathogen. Invasive fusariosis is a recognized complication in patients with hematological malignancies; however, proven infection caused by F. brachygibbosum has not previously been described. We report the first case of proven breakthrough sinusitis in a pediatric female with refractory acute myeloblastic leukaemia (AML) receiving posaconazole prophylaxis. Methods We describe the clinical presentation, microbiological diagnosis, antifungal susceptibility profile, treatment, and outcome of a 13-year-old neutropenic female with refractory AML who developed invasive fungal sinusitis. Species identification was established by Sanger sequencing of the elongation factor 1-alpha, and antifungal susceptibility testing was performed according to the EUCAST reference method. Results Computed tomography revealed extensive paranasal sinus involvement, and direct microscopy of sinus tissue demonstrated hyaline septate hyphae. Culture yielded a mould initially misidentified by MALDI-TOF MS as F. chlamydosporium. Molecular sequencing confirmed F. brachygibbosum. The isolate exhibited elevated Minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) to amphotericin B, azoles, echinocandins, and olorofim, while fosmanogepix showed a lower in vitro MIC. Extensive surgical debridement combined with liposomal amphotericin B, voriconazole, and subsequently olorofim was performed. Despite local control of the sinonasal infection and no microbiological or histopathological evidence of dissemination, the patient died 23 days after diagnosis. The death occurred in the context of progressive refractory AML, invasive fungal disease, pulmonary abnormalities, and subsequent neutropenic complications. Conclusion This report represents the first proven pediatric case of invasive sinusitis caused by F. brachygibbosum (FSAMSC) isolate with higher MICs to classical antifungals. The case highlights the diagnostic limitations of MALDI-TOF MS for rare Fusarium species, the value of molecular identification and antifungal susceptibility testing, and the emergence of environmental moulds breakthrough fungal infections. It also underscores the urgent need for effective novel antifungal agents against resistant Fusarium species.

title: Multimodal MRI fusion and three-dimensional reconstruction for preoperative assessment of neurovascular compression in trigeminal neuralgia: A retrospective study.
abstract: Background Microvascular decompression is the primary surgical intervention for trigeminal neuralgia aimed at resolving neurovascular compression. Given the potential surgical risks, accurate preoperative assessment of neurovascular compression is critical. Although 3D visualization has been applied to preoperative assessment of neurovascular relationships, quantitative evaluation of the trigeminal nerve-vessel relationship and its association with intraoperative NVC findings remains limited. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed data from trigeminal neuralgia patients, hemifacial spasm controls and healthy controls. Preoperative 3D-FIESTA and 3D-TOF-MRA data were acquired and processed for 3D fusion reconstruction using 3D Slicer. After validating the model's reliability against intraoperative findings, trigeminal nerves were stratified into four subgroups. Anatomical morphological parameters and neurovascular relationships were quantitatively measured and compared among the subgroups. Immediate postoperative outcomes in trigeminal neuralgia patients were also evaluated. Results A total of 92 trigeminal neuralgia patients, 99 hemifacial spasm controls and 30 healthy controls were enrolled. The trigeminal neuralgia cohort was significantly older than the control group (63.1 vs. 54.3 years, P < 0.05). The preoperative 3D reconstruction demonstrated high consistency with intraoperative findings (accuracy: 93%, Kappa: 0.89). ROC analysis identified an optimal neurovascular distance threshold of 1.23 mm for predicting intraoperative neurovascular compression (AUC = 0.957). Morphological analysis showed no significant intergroup difference in nerve diameter (P = 0.458), whereas cisternal length differed significantly among the five groups (P < 0.001). The TNS group showed the shortest mean neurovascular distance (1.1 mm, P < 0.001) and the highest prevalence of neurovascular compression (NVC) (79.3%, P < 0.001). These findings remained consistent after inclusion of healthy controls. Immediate postoperative outcomes were not significantly associated with intraoperative NVC status or the 1.23-mm neurovascular distance. Conclusion This study confirmed the high diagnostic accuracy of preoperative 3D MRI fusion. Crucially, a neurovascular distance threshold of 1.23 mm was identified as an exploratory imaging marker for definite intraoperative compression. However, this threshold should not be regarded as an independent criterion for treatment selection.

Microvascular decompression is the primary surgical intervention for trigeminal neuralgia aimed at resolving neurovascular compression. Given the potential surgical risks, accurate preoperative assessment of neurovascular compression is critical. Although 3D visualization has been applied to preoperative assessment of neurovascular relationships, quantitative evaluation of the trigeminal nerve-vessel relationship and its association with intraoperative NVC findings remains limited.

Materials and methods

We retrospectively analyzed data from trigeminal neuralgia patients, hemifacial spasm controls and healthy controls. Preoperative 3D-FIESTA and 3D-TOF-MRA data were acquired and processed for 3D fusion reconstruction using 3D Slicer. After validating the model's reliability against intraoperative findings, trigeminal nerves were stratified into four subgroups. Anatomical morphological parameters and neurovascular relationships were quantitatively measured and compared among the subgroups. Immediate postoperative outcomes in trigeminal neuralgia patients were also evaluated.

Results

A total of 92 trigeminal neuralgia patients, 99 hemifacial spasm controls and 30 healthy controls were enrolled. The trigeminal neuralgia cohort was significantly older than the control group (63.1 vs. 54.3 years, P < 0.05). The preoperative 3D reconstruction demonstrated high consistency with intraoperative findings (accuracy: 93%, Kappa: 0.89). ROC analysis identified an optimal neurovascular distance threshold of 1.23 mm for predicting intraoperative neurovascular compression (AUC = 0.957). Morphological analysis showed no significant intergroup difference in nerve diameter (P = 0.458), whereas cisternal length differed significantly among the five groups (P < 0.001). The TNS group showed the shortest mean neurovascular distance (1.1 mm, P < 0.001) and the highest prevalence of neurovascular compression (NVC) (79.3%, P < 0.001). These findings remained consistent after inclusion of healthy controls. Immediate postoperative outcomes were not significantly associated with intraoperative NVC status or the 1.23-mm neurovascular distance.

Conclusion

This study confirmed the high diagnostic accuracy of preoperative 3D MRI fusion. Crucially, a neurovascular distance threshold of 1.23 mm was identified as an exploratory imaging marker for definite intraoperative compression. However, this threshold should not be regarded as an independent criterion for treatment selection.

title: Foundation Models and Multimodal Learning for Medical Data with Applications in Oncology.
abstract: The rapid expansion of medical data, including radiological imaging, digital pathology, molecular profiling, electronic health records, and longitudinal clinical narratives, has created new opportunities for AI in healthcare, while also exposing the limitations of traditional unimodal modeling approaches. Multimodal learning addresses these challenges by integrating heterogeneous data sources, and recent advances in foundation models, large-scale pretrained models designed for broad task transfer, have further accelerated this shift. Together, these developments have given rise to multimodal foundation models that aim to learn generalizable, aligned representations across diverse clinical modalities. In this review, we provide an overview of multimodal foundation models in medical AI, with a particular focus on oncology. We first outline key medical data modalities and the machine learning objectives that motivate multimodal integration, including predictive, representational, and alignment-based goals. We then examine core architectural design patterns and training paradigms underlying multimodal foundation models, such as modality-specific encoders, fusion strategies, attention mechanisms, contrastive pretraining, and scalable self-supervised learning. Building on this foundation, we survey representative multimodal models across radiology, pathology, clinical text, and molecular domains. We further review applications of multimodal foundation models across the cancer care continuum, including early detection, diagnosis and subtyping, prognosis, therapy response prediction, and longitudinal survival modeling. Finally, we discuss critical challenges that limit clinical translation, including cross-institutional heterogeneity, temporal misalignment across modalities, weak supervision, interpretability, regulatory constraints, and workflow integration, and outline future directions for advancing safe and effective deployment in real-world oncology practice.

title: HCF-Net: a Hierarchical Cascade Fusion Network Aligned with Clinical Treatment Pathways for Preoperative Molecular Subtyping of Breast Cancer on Dynamic Contrast-Enhanced MRI.
abstract: Preoperative molecular subtyping of breast cancer is essential for treatment selection and prognosis assessment, yet most deep learning approaches formulate subtype prediction as a conventional flat multi-class task without reflecting the sequential clinical decision process. We developed HCF-Net, a hierarchical cascade fusion network that decomposes subtype prediction into three clinically aligned binary decision nodes and integrates multiphase DCE-MRI with clinicoradiologic information. The model was retrospectively developed and validated using a dual-center cohort of 373 women who underwent preoperative 3.0 T multiphase DCE-MRI. On an independent test set (n = 75), HCF-Net achieved a Macro-AUC of 0.868 (95% CI, 0.806-0.923), accuracy of 73.3%, Macro-F1 of 0.732, and Cohen's κ of 0.631. The fusion model consistently achieved the highest AUC across all three hierarchical decision nodes, reaching 0.890 for luminal versus non-luminal tumors, 0.865 for Luminal A versus Luminal B tumors, and 0.974 for HER2-enriched versus triple-negative tumors. The same ordering of classification strategies was observed with a ConvNeXt-Tiny backbone. Compared with conventional flat classification strategies, hierarchical cascade decomposition and decision-level fusion provided substantial performance gains. These findings suggest that a hierarchical fusion framework aligned with clinical decision pathways may provide an effective and interpretable approach for preoperative breast cancer molecular subtype prediction.

title: Complementary Error Profiles of Human Readers and Large Language Models in Detecting AI-Generated Chest Radiographs: A Comparative Reader Study.
abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) and diffusion models can generate realistic chest radiographs, raising concerns for dataset integrity when provenance metadata are absent. We compared authenticity judgments by two radiologists, two nonradiologist physicians, and three frontier LLMs (GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.5 Flash, Claude Opus 4.8) on 160 posteroanterior radiographs: 40 real NIH ChestX-ray14 images and 120 synthetic images generated from text by three pipelines. Each evaluator judged every image once; the LLM evaluation was repeated twice 3 months later. Balanced accuracy was the primary metric, given 75% synthetic prevalence. The two best evaluators reached nearly identical balanced accuracy from opposite operating points: Gemini 3.5 Flash had the highest point estimate (77.9%; specificity 100%, sensitivity 55.8%) and RAD1 was a close second (75.8%; specificity 55.0%, sensitivity 96.7%), a paired difference of - 2.1 percentage points (95% CI, - 5.8 to 1.2). On repetition, LLM judgments were not fully reproducible and this ordering did not hold. Nonradiologists performed near chance. All four human readers detected diffusion-generated images at 82-100%, whereas the radiologists misclassified 38-45% of real images and the conservative LLMs reached perfect specificity yet detected only 32-72% of LLM-generated images. With laterality markers and borders masked, specificity was 62.5% (Gemini) and 85.0% (GPT-5.5) against 90-100% in same-day unmasked runs. Interevaluator agreement was low throughout (Fleiss' kappa among LLMs 0.213). A frequency-domain baseline reached 98.3% balanced accuracy within this dataset but 12% sensitivity on a held-out generator. Human readers and LLMs failed on different images; visual authenticity assessment alone may be insufficient for provenance verification.

title: Development and External Testing of an Interpretable MRI-Based Machine Learning Model for Differentiating Endometrial Stromal Sarcoma from Cellular Leiomyoma.
abstract: This retrospective two-center diagnostic study was aimed at developing and externally testing an interpretable MRI-based machine learning model for differentiating endometrial stromal sarcoma (ESS) from cellular leiomyoma (CL). A total of 155 women with pathologically confirmed ESS or CL were assigned to a derivation cohort (n = 111) and an external testing cohort (n = 44). Clinical variables, qualitative MRI features, and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) histogram parameters were evaluated. Three MRI-derived predictors-irregular tumor margin, cystic areas on T2-weighted imaging, and mean ADC-were used to train six classifiers. The final support vector machine model with a radial basis function kernel was evaluated at a fixed threshold determined in the derivation cohort using receiver operating characteristic, calibration, decision curve, and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analyses. A reader study assessed the effect of model assistance. The model achieved areas under the curve of 0.843 (95% CI, 0.760-0.917) in the derivation cohort and 0.835 (95% CI, 0.669-0.960) in the external testing cohort. Calibration and decision curve analyses indicated acceptable performance and potential clinical utility. In an exploratory model-assisted reader analysis, junior radiologist specificity increased from 46.4 to 82.1% and accuracy from 52.3 to 77.3%. This interpretable three-feature model demonstrated promising performance across cohorts and may serve as an adjunctive tool for preoperative MRI assessment, although prospective multicenter validation is warranted.

title: Generalizability of Deep Learning Architectures for Oral Squamous Cell Carcinoma Classification in Histopathology: A Comparative CNN-Vision Transformer Study with External Validation and Label-Quality Analysis.
abstract: Oral squamous cell carcinoma (OSCC) is the most prevalent oral malignancy, with delayed diagnosis contributing to poor survival. Deep learning has shown promise for histopathological detection of OSCC, but reported performance is frequently based on single-source datasets, with limited external validation and variable annotation quality. Our study was to compare representative CNN and transformer architectures for histopathological OSCC classification and assess their generalizability under external domain shift. A total of 10,817 H&E-stained image patches from 114 patients were classified as OSCC or normal/control. Images were independently reviewed by two oral pathologists, with discordant cases adjudicated by a senior pathologist (Cohen's κ = 0.975). Eight ImageNet-pre-trained architectures (ResNet18, ResNet50, ResNet101, DenseNet121, EfficientNet-B0, ConvNeXt-Tiny, ViT-B/16, and Swin-T) were fine-tuned using three random seeds. Models were trained, validated, and tested on the internally curated dataset {MIDAS} and subsequently evaluated on two independent external datasets used exclusively for external validation. Diagnostic performance, computational efficiency, statistical significance, and model interpretability were assessed. To investigate the observed reduction in external performance, cancer-labelled images from the external datasets underwent post hoc expert pathological review for potential label discordance. title: Interpretable Source-Aware Bone-Muscle Fusion Framework for Multicenter Prediction of Osteoporotic Vertebral Fractures.
abstract: Osteoporotic vertebral fracture (OVF) is underrecognized, and bone mineral density (BMD) alone may be insufficient for prediction. We developed the multisource fusion model for osteoporotic vertebral fracture (MSF-OVF), an interpretable source-aware framework integrating clinical-demographic variables, BMD, and lumbar MRI-derived ventral and dorsal paraspinal muscle (PM) representations. This retrospective multicenter study included 2680 participants aged > 40 years from five centers (one training, one internal validation, four external test cohorts). Deep features from four PM regions were extracted using vision foundation model-guided transfer learning and integrated with age, sex, body mass index, and BMD through source-aware latent fusion. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), net reclassification improvement (NRI), calibration, and interpretability analyses. MSF-OVF achieved an AUC of 0.881 (95% CI, 0.854-0.909) in internal validation and 0.851-0.917 across four external cohorts. Compared with the clinical-demographic and BMD baseline, MSF-OVF improved AUC by 0.046-0.093 and significantly outperformed it in internal validation and most external cohorts (DeLong P ≤ 0.034). Continuous NRI was 0.268-1.034 across all validation cohorts (P ≤ 0.011). MSF-OVF also outperformed single-muscle models (AUC, 0.454-0.736; P ≤ 0.009). After training-derived logistic recalibration, the internal validation Brier score was 0.140, with a calibration-in-the-large (CITL) of - 0.168 and calibration slope of 0.926. Class activation maps mainly highlighted PM regions. Automated segmentation took several seconds and inference 57.71 ± 18.66 ms per participant. Source-aware fusion of clinical-demographic, BMD, and PM MRI information may support computer-aided multicenter OVF prediction.

title: Deep Learning-Based Automated Computed Tomography Classification of Posterior Malleolar Fractures for a Standardized Diagnostic Framework.
abstract: Despite advances in computed tomography (CT)-based classification systems for posterior malleolar fractures (PMFs), diagnostic consistency remains limited because these systems are still highly dependent on the observer's experience. This study aimed to develop a deep learning-based automated model capable of classifying PMFs according to the Haraguchi, Mason-Molloy, and Bartoníček-Rammelt clasification systems using CT scans, and to compare the classification performance of different convolutional neural network architectures. Retrospectively collected preoperative CT data from 480 adult patients with PMFs were analyzed. A total of 2398 CT slices were independently classified by three orthopedic surgeons according to the three classification systems, and majority consensus was used as the reference standard. Anonymized DICOM images were evaluated using VGG-16, ResNet-101, and DenseNet-121 architectures. The dataset was divided into 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% testing subsets. Model performance was assessed using accuracy, sensitivity, precision, F1 score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). The VGG-16 and ResNet-101 models demonstrated high classification performance in the Haraguchi and Mason-Molloy systems. In the VGG-16 model, AUC values exceeded 0.90 across most fracture subtypes, reaching particularly high levels in Haraguchi types I-III, Mason-Molloy types IIB and III, and Bartoníček-Rammelt type IV. Similarly, the ResNet-101 model achieved AUC values above 0.90 in most classes, with very high discriminative performance observed in selected subtypes. F1-scores were greater than 0.70 among most fracture categories and exceeded 0.80 in several, indicating strong and consistent classification performance. These findings demonstrate that deep learning-based automated CT classification of PMFs is feasible and diagnostically robust. The proposed framework may improve diagnostic consistency, reduce observer-dependent variability, and support standardized assessment of posterior malleolar fractures in clinical practice.

title: Explainability and Clinical Trust of Deep Learning in Glioblastoma Treatment Efficacy Prediction: A Comprehensive Framework.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) treatment response is highly heterogeneous. Predicting outcomes from pre-treatment MRI is a critical unmet need, yet the clinical adoption of "black box" deep learning (DL) models is hindered by a lack of transparency. Robust and holistic validation frameworks still need to be developed to allow clinical trust. A multi-layered eXplainable AI (XAI) pipeline was employed to dissect a previously developed deep learning model trained to predict GBM overall survival. First, the model's visual focus was qualitatively and quantitatively analysed. Second, the model's feature dependence was quantified using input ablation studies. Third, the depth at which class information becomes decodable was traced by linear probing of the internal representations. Finally, the clinical impact of the AI and its explanations was assessed in a multi-reader, multi-case study (37 patients, 4 readers, 3 phases, 444 observations) using Generalised Estimating Equations (GEE) and clustered bootstrapping. Analysis revealed a high-intensity heuristic: hyper-intense pixels at the skull periphery anchored "Long-Term" predictions, while the model defaulted to "Short-Term" based on tumour enhancement in its absence. The ablation study established this dependence, and linear probing pointed in the same direction. In the clinical study, AI assistance significantly improved expert accuracy (OR 1.598, p < 0.01) without artificially boosting confidence (p = 0.561). Importantly, the addition of XAI heatmaps was associated with a change in how experts used the AI score (interaction p < 0.01), and with fewer patients wrongly called long-term survivors. High predictive accuracy can mask reliance on low-level intensity heuristics. While superficial interpretation of saliency maps is perilous, multi-layered audits expose these shortcuts. Clinically, spatial heatmaps were associated with improved expert diagnostic accuracy and a shift in decision-making strategy.

title: From Intra- to Inter-habitat Analysis: Spatial Structure Features for Axillary Lymph Node Metastasis Prediction on Breast DCE-MRI.
abstract: Habitat radiomics characterizes texture within tumor subregions but discards the spatial relationships between them. We developed a landscape-ecology-inspired framework quantifying inter-habitat spatial structure on DCE-MRI, evaluated its complementary value alongside within-habitat radiomics, and compared early versus late fusion, using axillary lymph node metastasis (ALNM) prediction as the evaluation task. In this multicenter retrospective study, 284 patients from one center were randomly split into training (n = 198) and validation (n = 86) cohorts, with 120 patients from an independent institution as the external test set. Tumors were partitioned into six habitats by k-means clustering of 19 voxel-wise texture descriptors, with centroids derived exclusively from the training cohort. title: Semi-Automated Image Labeling and Object Tracking for MR-Guided Radiotherapy Using a Foundation Vision Model.
abstract: Magnetic resonance-guided radiotherapy (MRgRT) enables real-time tracking of tumor and organ motion for more precise radiation delivery. However, existing clinical tracking software struggles with high-velocity or non-rigid motion. Foundation models, such as Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) and MedSAM2, offer robust tracking with fast inference speeds and strong zero-shot accuracy that can improve with fine-tuning. Fine-tuning typically uses expert-labeled datasets, which are expensive to acquire. We explored SAM2's utility in accelerating the labeling process by developing a workflow where novices label < 1% of frames and SAM2 automatically labels the rest. We then evaluated SAM2 and MedSAM2 for tumor tracking on an open-access MRgRT dataset in three configurations: zero-shot, fine-tuned using manually labeled data, and fine-tuned using the semi-automatically labeled data. We measured accuracy with the Dice similarity coefficient, 95th percentile (P95) Hausdorff distance, and centroid distance. MedSAM2 and SAM2 demonstrated strong zero-shot tracking accuracy with no significant difference among the model variants. Fine-tuning significantly improved Dice coefficients (0.874 to 0.891, p = 0.006), P95 Hausdorff distances (9.069 to 4.378 mm, p < 0.001), and centroid distances (5.299 to 1.769 mm, p < 0.001) relative to zero-shot, with no significant difference between using manually labeled and semi-automatically labeled data. Therefore, leveraging SAM2 to semi-automatically generate labeled training data can substantially reduce the cost of data curation and long-term model maintenance without compromising accuracy.

title: CSNet: Cognitive Simulation Network for Reliable Histopathology-Based Cancer Diagnosis.
abstract: Histopathology-based cancer diagnosis is crucial for early detection and timely therapeutic intervention. However, most deep learning methods for histopathological image classification are mainly optimized as prediction models, with limited consideration of clinical diagnostic workflows. In routine practice, pathologists usually follow a sequential reasoning process: coarse assessment of possible abnormalities, detailed inspection of suspicious regions, and consultation-based reasoning to reduce uncertainty. To provide more reliable and interpretable decision support for histopathology-based cancer diagnosis, we propose the cognitive simulation network (CSNet), which draws inspiration from pathologists' sequential diagnostic workflow. First, the multi-view fuzzy assessment module integrates frequency, texture, and gradient cues through learnable fuzzy membership functions to estimate view-level abnormality degrees, providing an initial assessment of suspicious pathological evidence. Guided by this assessment, the gradient-guided fuzzy modulator converts abnormality information into spatial guidance, enhancing informative high-gradient morphological responses while suppressing redundant low-informative regions. Based on the modulated representations, the uncertainty-guided multi-expert synergy mechanism estimates diagnostic uncertainty and coordinates multiple expert branches to generate consensus representations for reliable prediction. Extensive experiments on Kather-5 K, LC25000, LC25000-clean, and a collected cervical cancer histopathology dataset demonstrate that CSNet achieves superior performance, with accuracies of 97.673%, 99.964%, 97.920%, and 99.861%, respectively. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the proposed designs, and statistical analyses confirm the reliability of the observed improvements. Meanwhile, robustness evaluations and comparative visualizations demonstrate stable performance and more consistent responses in diagnostically relevant tissue regions, highlighting the potential of CSNet for reliable histopathology-based cancer diagnosis.

title: Comparison of the Performances of Deep Learning Methods in Kellgren-Lawrence Classification of Knee Osteoarthritis: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: Knee osteoarthritis (OA) causes symptoms such as pain, stiffness, and functional limitation in the knees; plain knee radiographs are used in addition to physical examination in its diagnosis. This study aimed to compare the performance of pre-trained deep learning models in knee OA classification and to examine the effects of lateral knee radiographs and patient clinical data on the performance of these models. Eight centers participated in the study; radiographs from six centers were used for training, validation, and testing of the models, and radiographs from two centers were used for external validation. In addition to anteroposterior (AP) and lateral knee radiographs, clinical information such as age, gender, height, and weight was collected from the patients. A total of 1550 patients were included in the study. The performance of deep learning models VGG-16, ResNet-50, DenseNet-121, Inception_v3, and EfficientNetb0 was compared in the classification of knee OA. The VGG-16 model yielded significantly higher performance metrics than competing architectures (p < 0.001), with an accuracy of 0.73, sensitivity of 0.72, specificity of 0.93, F1 score of 0.72, positive predictive value (PPV) of 0.72, quadratic weighted Kappa of 0.91, and AUC of 0.93. Feature extraction was performed using the VGG-16 model, and the patient's age, gender, and BMI clinical characteristics were added to the image feature set and classified using machine learning algorithms. The XGBoost classifier showed statistically insignificant improvements of 1-2% in performance metrics. Similar performance results were obtained with the VGG-16 model in a study using only AP knee radiographs. Radiographs from two centers were used for external validation, and the VGG-16 model yielded accuracy of 0.65, sensitivity of 0.65, specificity of 0.91, PPV of 0.67, F1 score of 0.65, quadratic weighted kappa of 0.88, and AUC of 0.90. Adding age, gender, and BMI clinical characteristics to the knee radiograph image feature set did not significantly improve model performance. Furthermore, adding lateral radiographs to the AP knee radiograph set did not provide any additional contribution to KL classification performance.

title: AI-based Hip Fracture Classification from Pelvic X-ray Images Using a Hybrid PEFT-ViT and XGBoost Model.
abstract: Accurate radiographic classification of hip fractures into femoral neck (intracapsular) versus intertrochanteric (extracapsular) types is essential for surgical planning, yet most AI studies focus on binary detection using large datasets from high-resource regions, with no prior work from the Middle East. This study proposes a Hybrid PEFT-ViT and XGBoost framework for three-class classification of hip radiographs (Normal, Intertrochanteric fracture, Neck of femur fracture), using 768 X-ray images collected from King Abdullah University Hospital (KAUH) in Northern Jordan. A LoRA-fine-tuned ViT-Base/16 backbone extracted fused class-token and patch-token features, which were classified using XGBoost. On an independent test set of 77 radiographs, the proposed model achieved an accuracy of 88.31% (95% CI 79.3-93.7%), a sensitivity of 87.75%, a specificity of 94.28%, and an F1-score of 87.75%, the highest among the evaluated CNN-based (MobileNetV2, DenseNet121) and transformer-based (ViT, DeiT, Swin) baselines. These results show that clinically meaningful hip fracture classification can be achieved using a single-center dataset, providing a practical framework for resource-limited settings, although external validation is still required.

title: Validation of a Deep Learning Model for Automated Ureteral Length Measurement on CT Against Gross Specimens.
abstract: This study validates a deep learning model for automated ureteral length measurement on CT using gross specimen measurements as the reference standard. A deep learning model was trained on 3629 CT series from 1502 patients (cohort 1) to segment the ureter and extract centerline length. An independent prospective cohort (cohort 2) of 70 patients undergoing radical nephroureterectomy served as the hold-out test set. Each gross specimen was measured twice by one urologist (D1_length and D2_length), with their mean as the reference length (Ref_length). Model-predicted lengths (AI_length) were compared with Ref_length using repeated-measures one-way ANOVA with Tukey post hoc tests. Determinants of discrepancy were assessed with Spearman correlation and multiple linear regression. Marginal means (± SE) were 266 ± 3.85 mm (D1_length), 273 ± 3.25 mm (D2_length), 269 ± 2.75 mm (AI_length), and 269 ± 3.45 mm (Ref_length). Measurement method had a statistically significant but negligible effect on length (F(3, 207) = 2.73, p = 0.045, η 2 G = 0.007). D1_length and D2_length differed significantly from Ref_length (both p = 0.002), whereas AI_length was not statistically different from Ref_length (p > 0.999). In regression analysis, reference ureteral length was the only independently associated variable (coefficient - 0.54 mm per mm of reference length, 95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.39; p < 0.001); age, sex, body height, body weight, operation side, and lesion location were not significantly associated. The proposed deep learning pipeline achieved accurate fully automated ureteral segmentation and length measurement across diverse CT acquisition phases and demonstrated close agreement with surgical gross specimen measurements in a prospective clinical cohort, supporting its potential to assist preoperative planning and reduce reliance on manual measurement. The measurement discrepancy was governed primarily by ureteral length itself-with a small systematic underestimation in longer ureters-rather than by patient or procedural factors. However, this tendency, together with the single-center design, and the modest size of the prospective cohort, warrants further multicenter validation before routine clinical deployment.

Marginal means (± SE) were 266 ± 3.85 mm (D1_length), 273 ± 3.25 mm (D2_length), 269 ± 2.75 mm (AI_length), and 269 ± 3.45 mm (Ref_length). Measurement method had a statistically significant but negligible effect on length (F(3, 207) = 2.73, p = 0.045, η<sup>2</sup>G = 0.007). D1_length and D2_length differed significantly from Ref_length (both p = 0.002), whereas AI_length was not statistically different from Ref_length (p > 0.999). In regression analysis, reference ureteral length was the only independently associated variable (coefficient - 0.54 mm per mm of reference length, 95% CI - 0.70 to - 0.39; p < 0.001); age, sex, body height, body weight, operation side, and lesion location were not significantly associated. The proposed deep learning pipeline achieved accurate fully automated ureteral segmentation and length measurement across diverse CT acquisition phases and demonstrated close agreement with surgical gross specimen measurements in a prospective clinical cohort, supporting its potential to assist preoperative planning and reduce reliance on manual measurement. The measurement discrepancy was governed primarily by ureteral length itself-with a small systematic underestimation in longer ureters-rather than by patient or procedural factors. However, this tendency, together with the single-center design, and the modest size of the prospective cohort, warrants further multicenter validation before routine clinical deployment.

title: Use of Machine Learning and Imaging to Predict Outcomes After Lumbar Spine Surgery: A Systematic Review.
abstract: Postoperative outcomes following lumbar spine surgery remain variable, and existing clinical risk stratification methods offer limited predictive accuracy. Advances in machine learning enable quantitative analysis of routinely acquired spinal imaging, creating opportunities to improve preoperative outcome prediction. However, the methodological quality and clinical readiness of imaging-based machine learning models in lumbar spine surgery have not been systematically evaluated. This systematic review followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. PubMed, Embase, and Scopus were searched through October 2025 for studies using machine learning models trained on imaging data (MRI, CT, or radiographs) to predict postoperative outcomes after lumbar spine surgery. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST). Twenty-six studies published between 2019 and 2025 met inclusion criteria. Most models predicted patient-reported or clinical outcomes, with fewer addressing complications, structural outcomes, or imaging-derived biomarkers. MRI was the predominant modality. Model discrimination was frequently moderate to high (median AUC, 0.83), though external validation and calibration reporting were uncommon. All studies demonstrated high risk of bias, primarily related to analysis and validation practices. Imaging-based machine learning models show promise for improving preoperative outcome prediction after lumbar spine surgery, but methodological limitations limit current clinical applicability. Greater emphasis on external validation, standardized outcomes, and prospective evaluation is needed to support safe translation into routine spine care.

title: Impact of different pre-processing methods combined with combat harmonization on the reproducibility of radiomics features in healthy human brain MRI.
abstract: Objective To explore the effect of different pre-processing methods combined with ComBat harmonization on improving the stability of MRI radiomic features in healthy human brains. Methods T1FLAIR and T2W scans from 416 healthy subjects across four MRI systems underwent seven pipelines (Original, N4, Z-Score, DTN, Nyul, WhiteStripe, RAVEL). SynthSeg segmented white/gray matter for 93 IBSI radiomic features. Stability was quantified via covariate-adjusted standardized scanner effect (d = β_scanner/σ_res, |d|< 0.2) with 95% bootstrap CIs, supplemented by PCA and LOOCV AUC. Friedman and post-hoc McNemar tests with Bonferroni correction compared pipelines. FDR-corrected partial correlations assessed retention of significant age and sex associations after ComBat. Results Raw data exhibited extremely low stability with substantial scanner-induced effects, while scanner classification AUC was close to 1.0. ComBat harmonization significantly improved stability across all pipelines and reduced AUC to near 0.5. Within this dataset, DTN_ComBat demonstrated consistently high stability; pairwise statistical comparisons indicated it showed more favourable stability performance relative to most other pipelines for the majority of tested contrasts, with stable proportions exceeding 90% across all sequences and tissues, and retained 75.0-100.0% of statistically significant age and sex-related associations. Conclusion Unprocessed brain MRI radiomic features exhibit poor cross‑scanner stability. Within this dataset, ComBat effectively reduces scanner‑related feature‑distribution differences, while preserving most statistically‑significant age and sex‑related associations. Among tested pre-processing pipelines, DTN_ComBat showed comparatively favourable performance under the present healthy‑brain MRI scanner‑protocol configurations.

title: Radiological features of peritumoral brain injury and neurological outcomes after glioma surgery: a prospective observational study.
abstract: Purpose Despite significant advances in glioma surgery, early postoperative neuroimaging frequently reveals signs of surgical brain injury (SBI). This prospective observational study aimed to investigate the incidence, radiological characteristics, neurological outcomes and risk factors of SBI following glioma resection. Methods Patients with newly diagnosed supratentorial gliomas who undergo tumor resection were prospectively enrolled. Serial MRI examinations were administrated early postoperative (≤ 72 h) and on postoperative days 7, 14 and 28 to assess the characteristics of infarction, edema and microhemorrhage. Neurological outcomes were evaluated using the modified Rankin Scale (mRS) at postoperative day 28. Results A total of 64 patients was included. Postoperative infarction was identified in 14 patients (21.9%), with all anatomically localized to the basal ganglia, thalamus, or insular regions. Intraoperative blood loss ≥ 300 mL was independently associated with postoperative infarction (Odd Ratio [OR]: 4.62, p = 0.035). Microhemorrhage was observed in 53.8% of patients. Peritumoral edema occurred in all cases and exhibited two distinct patterns: residual tumor-associated edema (n = 42) and de novo surgery-induced edema (n = 22). The average volume of tumor-associated edema decreased, whereas that of surgery-induced edema increased over time. Among the 53 patients who completed neurological outcome assessments, 13 developed disability (mRS ≥ 2). Risk factors were higher intraoperative blood loss (OR: 8.88, p = 0.013) and postoperative infarction (OR: 6.33, p = 0.031). Conclusion SBI, including infarction and edema, is common following glioma surgery and associated with adverse neurological outcomes. Meticulous intraoperative hemostatic management is essential to prevent postoperative infarction and even disability outcome.

title: Limited clinical value of routine PET/CT in early-stage breast cancer: a multicenter retrospective study.
abstract: Background Staging of breast cancer at diagnosis is essential for prognosis and guiding treatment decisions. The role of ^18F-FDG positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) in patients with asymptomatic early-stage breast cancer remains controversial because of the low prevalence of distant metastasis and risk of false-positive findings. Materials and methods This is a retrospective multicenter cohort study across three tertiary centers in Lebanon. Adult patients with newly diagnosed stage I or IIA breast cancer who underwent PET/CT for initial staging between January 2019 and December 2024 were included. Patients receiving neoadjuvant therapy prior to imaging or with more advanced disease were excluded. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize outcomes, including rates of disease upstaging and false-positive findings. Results A total of 435 patients were included. Most tumors were invasive ductal carcinoma (88.0%) and hormone receptor-positive (ER 88.5%, PR 81.4%), with HER2 positivity in 17.7%. PET/CT resulted in stage upstaging in 23 patients (5.3%), 12 patients upstaged to stage IIA, 5 to stage IIB, and 6 to stage IV. However, histopathology confirmed distant metastases in only 3 patients (0.7%, 3/435). Overall, upstaging was pathologically confirmed in 11 patients, whereas it was not confirmed in 12 patients, with the discordant cases being predominantly attributable to false-positive nodal findings. PET/CT findings led to treatment modification in only 0.9% (4/435) of the cohort. Conclusion In this cohort of asymptomatic patients with clinical stage I-IIA breast cancer, PET/CT rarely identifies additional metastatic disease and frequently results in false-positive findings. These results suggest a selective, risk-adapted use of PET/CT rather than routine staging in early-stage breast cancer, particularly in resource-constrained healthcare settings, and should be interpreted in the context of the study's retrospective design.

title: Wireless versus cart-based ultrasound in musculoskeletal and superficial soft-tissue imaging: a prospective blinded cross-over study.
abstract: Aim Wireless ultrasound probes are increasingly used in point-of-care settings, but their performance in musculoskeletal and superficial soft-tissue imaging remains incompletely defined. This study compared image quality and clinical-pragmatic performance of a wireless ultrasound probe with a high-end cart-based ultrasound system. Methods This prospective blinded cross-over study included 41 musculoskeletal or superficial soft-tissue anatomical regions examined in routine clinical practice. Each region was assessed with both the Mindray Resona I9 Elite Edition cart-based system and the Mindray TE-Air e5M wireless probe. Device order was randomized. Images were acquired by one experienced operator, anonymized, coded, and reviewed offline by an experienced reviewer blinded to device type. Image quality, anatomical margin definition, tissue contrast, speckle noise, diagnostic confidence, interpretability, diagnosis possibility, pathological finding detection, clinical decision sufficiency, and the need for further imaging were assessed. Results The cart-based system showed superior image quality. Median global image quality was 5 versus 3, anatomical margin definition 5 versus 3 and tissue contrast 5 versus 4. Diagnostic confidence was higher with the cart-based system, 97.95 ± 5.32 versus 69.10 ± 16.05. Clinical-pragmatic endpoints showed a less pronounced reduction: examination interpretability was 97.6% versus 90.2%, diagnosis was considered possible in 73.2% versus 61.0%, and images were sufficient for clinical decision-making in 70.7% versus 58.5%. Conclusions The wireless probe provided lower image quality and confidence but retained clinically useful performance in selected cases. It should be considered complementary rather than a substitute for high-end cart-based ultrasound.

title: Comparison of Integrated Versus Sequential Artificial Intelligence-Based Computer-Aided Diagnosis Systems in Breast Ultrasound: A Prospective Pilot Study on Examination Time, Reproducibility, and Diagnostic Performance.
abstract: Rationale and objectives To compare integrated and sequential artificial intelligence-based computer-aided diagnosis (AI-CAD) systems in terms of examination time, reproducibility, and diagnostic performance in breast ultrasound (US). Materials and methods This prospective single-center study included women who underwent breast US at a breast imaging center between February and March 2025. Two real-time AI-CAD systems were evaluated: an integrated system providing simultaneous lesion detection and diagnosis during scanning, and a sequential system in which lesion detection and diagnostic assessment were performed separately. Examination time was assessed in patients who underwent paired breast US examinations with both AI-CAD systems during the same visit, with randomized examination order. Reproducibility was assessed by applying both systems twice to the same breast lesions. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using sensitivity, specificity, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results Examination time analysis included 97 patients and showed longer examination time with sequential AI-CAD than with integrated AI-CAD (P < .001), regardless of examination order. Reproducibility analysis included 145 patients with 215 lesions and showed almost perfect agreement between the first and second acquisitions for both systems (integrated vs. sequential: κ = 0.81 vs. 0.83). For the comparison between the first and second acquisitions, κ values for the integrated versus sequential systems were 0.92 versus 0.76 for malignant lesions, 0.79 versus 0.84 for mass lesions, and 1.00 versus 0.75 for nonmass lesions. However, agreement patterns varied across other scan-plane comparisons. Diagnostic performance analysis included 242 patients. Integrated AI-CAD showed higher sensitivity (integrated vs. sequential: 87.6% vs. 76.9%; P < .001), whereas sequential AI-CAD showed higher specificity (integrated vs. sequential: 74.2% vs. 90.0%; P < .001). AUC did not differ between the two systems. Conclusion Integrated and sequential AI-CAD systems showed complementary strengths in breast US. Integrated AI-CAD favored shorter examination time and higher sensitivity, whereas sequential AI-CAD favored higher specificity, with reproducibility differing according to lesion type.
